Empirical Research Plan: “The Causal Impact of Education on Earnings”

------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–Stage Least Squares (2SLS) Instrumental‐Variables (IV)

Justification  
• The core regressor (years of schooling) is choice–driven and likely correlated with unobservables that also affect earnings (ability, motivation, family background).  
• The cross-sectional Census contains no repeated observations of the same individual, so DID or event-study designs are infeasible.  
• Two well-documented sources of plausibly exogenous variation in schooling are available:  
  (i) Geographic proximity to colleges at age 17 (Card 1995 style)  
  (ii) Compulsory Schooling Law (CSL) reforms that raised the minimum school-leaving age (Angrist & Krueger 1991 style).  
• Both sources satisfy the standard IV moment conditions under reasonable assumptions, making 2SLS the work-horse strategy.

------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
SCHOOL_i = completed years of education for individual i (continuous).  
We estimate the marginal return to one additional year; treatment = being induced to complete more schooling.

Instruments  

Z1_i (“College proximity”): 1 = birth-county within 10 miles of a 4-year college that existed when the individual was age 17; 0 otherwise.  
Z2_i (“CSL exposure”): 1 = born in a state-×-birth-cohort for which a higher minimum school-leaving age law was binding; 0 otherwise. (Fuzzy RD across birth-cohort is embedded in this IV.)

Control group / counterfactual  
Individuals not exposed to either source of inducement (far from a college and non-binding CSL cohort). These people serve as the counterfactual earnings path absent exogenous boosts to schooling.

Timing  
• College-distance instrument is defined at age 17 (close to the schooling decision).  
• CSL instrument is indexed by birth year relative to the reform enactment; treatment occurs when the cohort reaches the new mandatory leaving age (≈ age 14–16).

------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance – Proximity and CSL exposure must increase schooling.  
  Plausibility: Both relationships are strongly documented; F-statistics > 10 expected.

A2. Exclusion – Instruments affect earnings only through schooling.  
  – College proximity must not mechanically raise local wages (address with county fixed effects, urban controls).  
  – CSL reforms should not directly change labor demand (address with state-×-year FE).

A3. Independence – Instruments are as-good-as-random conditional on covariates.  
  – Birth-county location predetermined relative to individual ability; still, control for parental SES proxies.  
  – CSL timing set by legislatures, arguably exogenous to any single cohort; include state trends.

A4. Monotonicity – No defiers: nobody goes to *less* school because a college opened nearby or the law changed.

A5. SUTVA – An individual’s earnings are unaffected by others’ treatment status (reasonable at national scale).

------------------------------------------------------
4. Most Salient Threats and Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selective migration: Families valuing education might move closer to colleges.  
Mitigation: Construct proximity from county of birth (not current residence); add mother’s education, race, and pre-treatment county characteristics.

T2. Local labor-market effects of colleges: Colleges boost area wages independent of schooling.  
Mitigation: Include county-of-residence fixed effects, local unemployment rate, urban/rural dummy; test “reduced-form” effect of instrument on wages *for people who did not increase schooling*.

T3. CSL correlation with unobserved state shocks (e.g., simultaneous child-labor laws).  
Mitigation: State-specific linear trends; add controls for other policy changes (minimum wage, child-labor statutes); placebo tests on pre-reform cohorts.

------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast 2SLS
library(sandwich)    # robust vcov
library(lmtest)

# 1. Load
census <- fread("census_education_earnings.csv")       # 1 row = individual

# 2. Construct variables
census[, ln_earn  := log(annual_income)]
census[, near_college := as.integer(distance_to_college <= 10)]     # Z1
census[, csl_exposed := as.integer(birth_year >= reform_year &      # Z2
                                   birth_year <  reform_year + 5)]  # 5-yr window

# main instrument: either one or both
census[, instruments := near_college + csl_exposed]    # okay if >1

# Controls
census[, ':='(age2 = age^2,
              black = (race == "Black"),
              hisp  = (hispanic == 1))]

# 3. Main 2SLS
iv_main <- feols(ln_earn ~ SCHOOL |                       # second stage
                 near_college + csl_exposed ~             # first stage instruments
                 age + age2 + male + black + hisp |       # FE
                 state + birth_year,                      # absorb state & cohort FE
                 data = census, cluster = ~state)

summary(iv_main, cluster = "state")

# 4. Robustness: only college instrument, restrict to movers unlikely
iv_robust <- feols(ln_earn ~ SCHOOL | near_college ~
                   age + age2 + male + black + hisp |
                   state + birth_year,
                   data = census[birth_state == current_state],      # stayers only
                   cluster = ~state)
summary(iv_robust, cluster = "state")

# 5. First-stage F-stat check
kable(iv_main$iv_first_stage$fsres)
```

------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (Mincer) predicts a positive return; prior empirical estimates for the U.S. suggest 7–10 % higher annual earnings per additional year of schooling. I therefore expect:  

β_IV ≈ 0.08 (log points) → roughly 8 % higher annual income per added year.

------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) ............. 1  
C2: Instrument exogenous given controls ............ 0.5  
C3: Exclusion restriction plausible ................ 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ...................... 1  
C5: SUTVA .......................................... 1  
Total (out of 5) ................................... 4.0

The partial scores on C2 and C3 reflect remaining concerns about selective migration and local labor-market spillovers, which are mitigated but not completely eliminated.
